chapter: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
title: Smiley Lewis in the band and why he gave up the band
summary: Smiley Lewis played guitar with his band and learned from the bassist; Crawford's band was praised but he could not afford to keep it.

bands.name: Sugar Boy and His Cane Cutters

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: And he played with your band. When you would go on stage he would accompany you and play guitar.
Was he a good guitar player?
He didn't play guitar on a lot of his records though.
No. I don't think he played guitar on any of his records really. I don't think. He may have. I don't think he played on any of his records. He wasn't a real, what you say, well.
He wasn't a way to go on stage. Guitar.

Yeah. But when he started playing with me and the guys in the band, he learned a whole lot from the guys in the band, especially Fields, the bass player, because Fields could play guitar. Fields could play guitar? Mm-hmm.
Did he ever play with you?
No, no, he never played with me.

He knew how and he taught Smiley a whole lot and I did too. Fields taught Smiley something. I did too. That's interesting. And somebody said he had been playing about 20 years or more and he learned more and a little while he played with me than he had in all the years he had been playing. Well, your band was always the favorite band of New Orleans, wasn't it? I don't know. In their 50s and everything. I don't know. That's what I hear. That's what Red Tyler and all of them say. I don't know. Everybody always liked your band the best. Always try to keep a good band. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I couldn't afford to keep the band together. So I just quit. See if I can't have what I want, well, I won't take anything.
